ground_truth_question: What is a Personal Data Incident under this policy, and can you give examples?
ground_truth_answer: A Personal Data Incident is a suspected adverse event—either accidental or intentional—in an information system, network, or resource, or even the threat of such an event, when it involves Personal Data or PHI. Examples include unauthorized use of another user’s account, misuse of system privileges, or running malicious code that destroys data. The term “incident” signals that harm has occurred or could occur.
exact_excerpt_from_policy: “Personal Data Incident: A suspected adverse event (accidental or intended) in an information system/network/resource, or the threat of the occurrence of such an event involving Personal Data and/or PHI. Examples of a Personal Data Incident include unauthorized use of another user’s account, unauthorized use of system privileges, and execution of malicious code that destroys data. ‘Incident’ implies harm, or the potential for harm.”

ground_truth_question: What qualifies as a Personal Data Breach?
ground_truth_answer: A Personal Data Breach is a confirmed security breach that leads to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure of, or access to Personal Data in transit, at rest, or otherwise processed. The concept also encompasses any breach of unsecured PHI under HIPAA.
exact_excerpt_from_policy: “Personal Data Breach: A confirmed breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure of, or access to, Personal Data transmitted, stored, or otherwise processed. ground_truth_question: How does the policy define a Breach of PHI?
ground_truth_answer: A Breach of PHI is an impermissible use or disclosure of PHI under HIPAA that compromises the security or privacy of that information. Such an impermissible use or disclosure is presumed to be a breach unless BCG can show there is a low probability the PHI has been compromised.
exact_excerpt_from_policy: “Breach of PHI: An impermissible use or disclosure of PHI under HIPAA which compromises the security or privacy of the PHI. The impermissible use of PHI is presumed to be a breach, unless it can be demonstrated by BCG that there is a low probability the PHI obtained has been compromised.”

ground_truth_question: Are there exceptions to what counts as a Breach of PHI?
ground_truth_answer: Yes. There are three exceptions: (1) unintentional acquisition, access, or use by someone within the authorized workforce or acting under the authority of a covered entity or business associate, when done in good faith and within scope; (2) an inadvertent disclosure by someone authorized to access PHI to another person also authorized to receive PHI within the same covered entity, business associate, or organized health care arrangement; and (3) when BCG has a good‑faith belief that the unauthorized recipient could not have retained the PHI.
exact_excerpt_from_policy: “There are three exceptions to this definition of ‘breach,’ which are as follows: I. The PHI was unintentionally acquired, accessed, or used by a workforce member or person acting under the authority of a covered entity or business associate, where such acquisition, access, or use, was made in good faith and within the scope of authority; II. The PHI was inadvertently disclosed by a person who had authorization to access the PHI, whether a covered entity or business associate, to another person who was also authorized to have access to PHI at the covered entity, business associate, or organized health care arrangement in which the covered entity participates; or III. The covered entity or business associate has good faith that the unauthorized person which the impermissible disclosure was made to, would not have been able to retain the PHI.”

ground_truth_question: What does the DPO assess to determine whether a breach is notifiable and what process is followed?
ground_truth_answer: After CSIRT’s evaluation, the DPO assesses whether the incident is likely to result in a risk or high risk to affected individuals’ rights and freedoms, or otherwise requires notification under applicable laws. If the DPO determines that a Notifiable Breach has occurred, BCG follows the notification procedures in the Cybersecurity Incident Response Plan (CIRP) to notify the relevant regulatory authority and affected individuals, and promptly responds without delay, consistent with the timeframes required under applicable data privacy laws.
exact_excerpt_from_policy: “Following this, the DPO will evaluate whether the incident is likely to result in a risk or high risk to the rights and freedoms of the affected individual(s) or otherwise may require notification to a regulatory authority or affected individual(s) under Applicable Data Privacy Laws (a “Notifiable Breach”), in accordance with the procedure outlined in BCG’s Cybersecurity Incident Response Plan (“CIRP”). Upon evaluation, if it is determined by the DPO that a Notifiable Breach has occurred, BCG will follow the notification procedures outlined in the CIRP to notify the regulatory authority and the affected individual(s) as required and promptly respond to the Personal Data Breach without delay and in accordance with the timeframes required under Applicable Data Privacy Laws.”

ground_truth_question: What factors must the HIPAA Security Officer consider when assessing whether a Breach of PHI has occurred?
ground_truth_answer: The HIPAA Security Officer must conduct a risk assessment that, at minimum, considers: whether any exception to the HIPAA “breach” definition applies; the nature and extent of PHI involved, including types of identifiers and the likelihood of re‑identification; who used or received the PHI; whether the PHI was actually acquired or viewed; the extent to which risk to the PHI has been mitigated; and that appropriate authorities and clients have been informed by the HIPAA Security Officer.
